To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the durations of the intervals during which hibernators are torpid or euthermic are dependent on body mass, and these relationships support the concept of metabolic control of hibernation.
small hibernators remain torpid for longer periods of time than large ones, but they also remain euthermic for shorter periods of time.

the durations of the intervals between bouts of torpor are proportional to body mass, the durations of torpor are inversely proportional to body mass and, in midwinter at least, the durations of the euthermic intervals are also inversely proportional to mass, although the proportional differences between species are small.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of why animals undergo seasonal changes in their activity levels.
the evolution of mammalian hibernators and their ability to survive in cold environments without food for long periods of time.
understanding the physiological and ecological consequences of seasonal changes in body temperature in mammals and birds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the durations of torpor and of euthermia during hibernation are determined by metabolic rates, and the durations of euthermic and torpid intervals are determined by the same metabolic process.

the timing of the changes in body temperature is determined by some metabolic process, but that the metabolic process is more complex than the simple metabolic control of arousal and that the process is not identical in all species.

, in mid-winter, hibernating mammals remain at high body temperature until a fixed metabolic imbalance has been restored, and that the duration of each torpor episode is dependent on the mass-specific rates of metabolism in torpor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the timing of the changes in body temperature during hibernation are controlled by some metabolic mechanism.
the timing of hibernation is controlled by some unknown metabolic process that is dependent on body mass.

the duration of each interval of torpor is controlled by some process that is independent of body mass, whereas the durations of intervals of euthermia are determined, at least in part, by some process that varies with body mass.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, at the level of the entire hibernation cycle, large hibernators are able to spend more time at high body temperature than small hibernator and thus are able to maintain a higher rate of metabolism during the winter than small hibernating species.
, in the middle of winter, small hibernators remain torpid longer and euthermic shorter than large hibernators.

, in hibernators that are able to hibernate at 5°C without food, the durations of torpor and of euthermia during hibernation are dependent on body mass, as predicted by the metabolic theory of mammalian hibernators, and the durations of the intervals during hibernation appear to be controlled by the metabolic process that controls body temperature changes.
